title: Presenting Vocabulary Meaning: Context, Pictures, and Realia
brief: Open by explaining the three core channels for presenting new word meaning—context, pictures, and realia—drawing directly on the 'How Do You Like to Learn?' activity list from the source, which enumerates options such as drawing pictures about words, labelling parts of a diagram, cutting out pictures representing words, disassembling a real object (e.g., a real computer), and making a computer model using cardboard. Use these concrete examples to show how each channel works in practice: context embeds the word in a meaningful situation (story, song, skit), pictures create a visual anchor, and realia (physical objects or models) give learners a tangible referent. Explain why offering multiple presentation channels matters by referencing the source's prompt about why it is important to give students choices about how they learn. Close by noting that teachers can gather information about student preferences and interests before selecting a presentation method.

title: Organising Words: Families, Collocations, and Topic Sets
brief: Explain three ways teachers can help learners organise new vocabulary into memorable networks: word families, collocations, and topic sets. Draw on the Create-to-Communicate scratchboard activity, specifically the instruction to 'emphasise to students that the collection of words all belong to a related group or category' after compiling the vocabulary list on the board—use this as a model for topic-set organisation. Reference the Word Bricks collection from Activate, which groups words by grammatical family (nouns, verbs, irregular past-tense verbs, modal verbs, prepositions, conjunctions, etc.) as printed in the List of Word Bricks, to illustrate how word-family sorting works in a classroom resource. Use the Activate guidance on adding function words (articles, auxiliaries, clause markers, prepositions) to show how collocational 'glue words' connect content vocabulary into complete structures. Conclude by advising teachers to keep an ongoing posted list of new words—as recommended in the Activate DIY section—so that topic sets grow organically from lessons.

title: Active Practice: Chain Stories and Word Poems
brief: Present two structured production activities drawn directly from Create-to-Communicate. First, describe the Chain Story activity in full: students are broken into groups of three or four; one member begins a sentence containing a vocabulary word; the next continues the story adding another vocabulary word; the process continues until every word on the board has been used; groups may repeat the activity to create a different chain story with the same words; volunteers then re-tell their stories to the class. Second, describe the Vocabulary Word Poem closing activity: students select one vocabulary word, write it vertically down their paper, and compose a word, phrase, or sentence for each letter—with the teacher choosing the appropriate option based on learner level. Emphasise that both activities require learners to use vocabulary productively rather than passively, and that the chain story can be repeated for additional practice with the same word set.

title: Games from the Activate Bank: Brick Bingo and Word Category Bingo
brief: Introduce two ready-to-use games from the Activate games bank. For Brick Bingo, explain that players build a 3×3 (or extended 4×4) card using Word Bricks of their choice, the teacher calls words, players remove matching bricks, and winning patterns include a full row, column, diagonal, or four corners; a round ends when one team removes all bricks and shouts 'White Out!' For Word Category Bingo, explain that it follows the same Bingo procedure but restricts card-building to one grammatical or lexical category—for example, Preposition Bingo requires players to find only prepositions in the collection; the source lists both basic categories (nouns, verbs, adjectives/adverbs, articles/pronouns, prepositions, words of three letters or fewer) and more challenging ones (countable nouns, irregular past-tense verbs, abstract words, words that can be both nouns and verbs). Note that the category choice controls difficulty, making Word Category Bingo adaptable across levels. Advise teachers to keep a master word list for these games as recommended in the Activate DIY section.

title: Games from the Activate Bank: Describe and Guess, and Word Category Sprint
brief: Present two further Activate games that build fluency and categorisation skills. For Describe and Guess, explain that players sit in groups of three to five, each player selects a Word Brick and describes the word without saying it aloud, and the remaining players try to guess the word—draw directly on the Activate instructions for this game. For the Word Category Sprint (the timed category-finding game described in the Activate source), explain that the teacher calls out a word category, starts a two-minute timer, teams search their set of Word Bricks for words matching that category, and at the end each team reports how many matching bricks they found; multiple rounds can be played by calling a new category each time. Note that the teacher may need to give examples of the category before starting the timer to ensure players understand what to look for. Together, these two games practise both receptive recognition (sprint) and productive description (Describe and Guess), covering different cognitive demands with the same physical materials.

title: Building and Expanding the Word Bricks Collection
brief: Explain how teachers and students can create and grow a classroom Word Bricks collection as a sustainable vocabulary resource, drawing entirely on the Activate DIY section. Describe the student-led brick-making procedure: groups brainstorm ten or more useful words (from the next textbook chapter or everyday events), the teacher checks for spelling accuracy and duplicates (or students alphabetise and cross-duplicate words on the board—noted in the source as a competitive activity in itself), each group is assigned a set of function words to include, and students write their words neatly on blank bricks. Stress the Activate guidance that function words—articles, auxiliaries, negatives, modals, prepositions, clause markers—must be added in sufficient quantity so learners can connect content words into complete sentences. Note that the collection is always changing: bricks are lost or become illegible, but the teacher can also add key vocabulary at the start of each new textbook chapter. Close by recommending that teachers keep a posted running list of words to add, and encourage students to bring in new words from outside the classroom.
